ignores_rate_changes.note: uses only the first rate in the schedule for the whole accrual period

ignores_grace_period.note: accrues interest starting the day after due_date, ignoring grace_period_days

always_actual_365.note: always divides by 365 regardless of the jurisdiction's day_count_convention

never_compounds.note: treats compounding as always simple, never capitalizes accrued interest

fee_threshold_off_by_one.note: triggers the late fee on due_date + threshold_days instead of + threshold_days + 1

allocation_principal_first.note: pays down principal before fees/interest regardless of the specified payment_allocation_order

rounds_daily.note: rounds each day's accrual to the cent instead of only the final total -- within the 5-cent tolerance, not a real bug worth penalizing

calibration.note: Each probe is a 'plausible but subtly wrong' implementation that gets exactly ONE rule interaction wrong while implementing everything else correctly -- not a strawman. The held-out scenario (85 queries: 14 hand-curated edge cases targeting specific rule interactions -- grace-period boundary, mid-window rate change, late-fee threshold boundary, fee-cap engagement, monthly compounding across February in both a leap and non-leap year, payment-allocation-order sensitivity, actual_365 vs actual_360, and a long-horizon rounding-drift check -- plus 70 independently generated random cases) was built specifically so that missing any one rule interaction fails a large, robust fraction of queries: worst adversarial probe reaches 82.4% correct, the reference reaches 100%, and the bar (81/85 = 95.3%) sits between them with a wide, non-noisy margin. Unlike two earlier task designs this session (a subset-sum-style partition problem and a bipartite matching problem), this is a correctness task, not an optimization-quality task -- there is no heuristic that can partially satisfy multiple rules at once and land in between; each bug is caught deterministically by specific queries that exercise it.
